units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Okay, it's evening. Where are we?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Outside the hotel, on the south side of the river, on Wacker Drive.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Head west, along the river, and let me prove that a road can be interesting.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: The bet.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The bet. Wacker Drive is named for Charles H.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Wacker, an early twentieth-century businessman and city planner.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The first section was completed in 1926 at a cost of eight million dollars.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It replaced two older streets, South Water Street and River Street.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Okay. Two streets became one. Not thrilling yet.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It's a double-decker road. There's an upper level, where you're standing, and a lower level for service vehicles, delivery trucks, waste collection and utilities.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So that's why Chicago has Lower Wacker.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Yes. If you've seen a movie car chase under Chicago, that's the same lower level.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Some sections have a third level too, used for towing, impound, utilities and railroad maintenance.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: A road with a basement and a sub-basement.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And the road follows the south bank of the main branch of the Chicago River through the Loop.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In the early 2000s the stretch from Michigan Avenue to Lake Street was redesigned with walkways along the river to be more pedestrian-friendly.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So we're walking on a redesign.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: We are.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Fine. A double-decker road is mildly interesting.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Mildly. Don't push it.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Noted. Keep going west to LaSalle Street, and the bridge.
